audit.reasoning: Coding (fixed-dominant final stress, final stress, not in the strict set) is correct and now doubly supported. (1) Quote: verbatim in DiCanio 2008 sec. 2.2.5, but on printed p.30, not 'p.20' as the locator says; no file was held before this reading — now. (2) Deciding source is weak in kind: a dissertation on a different Triqui variety giving a two-sentence second-hand summary of Hollenbach. (3) The primary fieldworker's own grammar (Hollenbach 2008 Gramática popular, ILV, 216 pp), downloaded now via the Internet Archive from SIL Mexico archives/35332, states the rule first-hand at sec. 2.6 p.15: every word is pronounced with greater force on the last syllable regardless of tonal pattern, with secondary stress on non-final syllables bearing tone 3 or 5; sec. 4.5 p.32 notes vocative nouns shift stress to an earlier syllable — an exception consistent with not in the strict set/dominant. Recommended: swap the decidi

sources.quote: In Copala Trique, Hollenbach observes that tone, the fortis-lenis consonant contrast, laryngeals, and vowel nasalization are maximally contrastive in word-final syllables. Copala Trique also has word-final vowel lengthening. ... The similar patterns among the three dialects suggest that final stress is a shared feature in the Trique languages.

sources.quote: p.15: 'En todas las palabras del triqui de Copala la última sílaba se pronuncia con mayor fuerza, tanto las que terminan con una vocal como las que terminan con una consonante, cualquiera que sea el patrón tonal. Así que, no es necesario escribir el acento. Las palabras que tienen el tono 3 o el tono 5 en una sílaba no final tienen un acento secundario en esta sílaba.' p.32: 'Cuando otros sustantivos se usan como vocativos, cambian el acento prosódico de la sílaba final a una sílaba anterior; y muchas veces su tono cambia.' (chu³vee³² '¡perro!' vs chuvee³ 'perro').
